e-455.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 0 \\ u & 2 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^0 x(x^2+1)^3\,\textrm{d}x=\int_2^1 u^3\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}{|}_{2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}-{2}^{4}}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1-16}{4} \\  & =-\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: Note that in this example, when we changed the limits the integral $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 \ldots \textrm{d}x$ became $\displaystyle \int_{2}^1 \ldots \textrm{d}u.$ When changing the limits, it is important to respect the order in which the limits are applied. The lower limit of the integral in $u$ must correspond to the lower limit of the integral in $x.$ Same for the upper limit.

content.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{({x}^{3}+1)}^{3}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u & ={\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({9}^{5/2}-{1}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(({3}^{2})^{5/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({3}^{5}-1) \\  & =\frac{484}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Evaluate the definite integral ∫1213x+2dx.

a
ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)
b
−ln⁡(2)−13ln⁡(5)
c
13ln⁡(2)−13ln⁡(5)
d
ln⁡(2)−13ln⁡(5)
e
−13ln⁡(2)−13ln⁡(5)
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=3x+2, so dx=du/3 and the limits become 5 and 8. The integral equals (ln(8)−ln(5))/3=ln(2)−ln(5)/3, which is option d.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =3x+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3 \\ \text{d}u & =3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3x+2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 1 & 2 \\ u & 5 & 8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{(3x+2)}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{5}^{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =3x+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3 \\ \text{d}u & =3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3x+2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 1 & 2 \\ u & 5 & 8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{(3x+2)}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{5}^{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =1+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ 2\,\text{d}u & =4x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+{x}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})}\cdot 4x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u & =2{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution
content.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =1+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ 2\,\text{d}u & =4x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+{x}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})}\cdot 4x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u & =2{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^4+9, so du=4x^3 dx and the limits become 9 and 25. The integral is (1/4)ln(25/9)=(1/2)ln(5/3), which is option e.

after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{4}+9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3} \\ \text{d}u & =4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & ={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{4}+9.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 9 & 25\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{({x}^{4}+9)}\,{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{9}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(25)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3}).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{4}+9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3} \\ \text{d}u & =4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & ={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{4}+9.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 9 & 25\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{({x}^{4}+9)}\,{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{9}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(25)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^3+2, so du=3x^2 dx. The limits become 1 and 3, giving (1/3)∫₁³du/u=(1/3)(ln(3)−ln(1))=(1/3)ln(3), which is option c.

after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & ={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}+2.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{({x}^{3}+2)}\,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$
